title: Application for a stay of execution of sentence of death

No. ___
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
______________________________________________
BRYAN F. JENNINGS,
Petitioner,
v.
STATE OF FLORIDA,
Respondent.
______________________________________________
On Petition for a Writ of Certiorari to the Supreme Court of Florida
______________________________________________________________
APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
______________________________________________________________
THIS IS A CAPITAL CASE 
EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR 
THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 13, 2025, at 6:00P.M.
______________________________________________
*ERIC C. PINKARD
FLORIDA BAR NO. 651443
LAW OFFICE OF THE CAPITAL COLLATERAL REGIONAL COUNSEL
12973 N. Telecom Parkway
Temple Terrace, Florida 33637
Phone No. (813) 558-1600 Ext. 603
Fax No. (813) 558-1601
Email: PINKARD@CCMR.STATE.FL.US
*COUNSEL OF RECORD

2
To the Honorable Clarence Thomas, Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of 
the United States:
The State of Florida has scheduled the execution of Petitioner, Bryan F. 
Jennings, for Thursday, November 13, 2025, at 6:00 p.m. The Florida Supreme Court 
denied state court relief as well as Mr. Jennings’ request for stay on November 6, 
2025. Mr. Jennings respectfully requests that this Court stay his execution, pursuant 
to Supreme Court Rule 23 and 28 U.S.C. § 2101(f), pending consideration of his 
concurrently filed petition for a writ of certiorari. 
STANDARDS FOR A STAY OF EXECUTION
The standards for granting a stay of execution are well established. Barefoot v. 
Estelle, 463 U.S. 880, 895 (1983). There “must be a reasonable probability that four 
members of the Court would consider the underlying issue sufficiently meritorious 
for the grant of certiorari or the notation of probable jurisdiction; there must be a 
significant possibility of reversal of the lower court’s decision; and there must be a 
likelihood that irreparable harm will result if that decision is not stayed.” Id. (quoting 
White v. Florida, 458 U.S. 1301, 1302 (1982) (Powell, J., in chambers).
PETITIONER SHOULD BE GRANTED A STAY OF EXECUTION
A stay of execution is warranted because the questions raised in Mr. Jennings’
petition for a writ of certiorari are substantial and meritorious. The petition presents 
serious constitutional questions that reach the core of this Court’s Eighth and 
Fourteenth Amendment jurisprudence and demand review before the State carries

3
out an irreversible execution. Furman v. Georgia, 408 U.S. 238 (1972); Gregg v. 
Georgia, 428 U.S. 153 (1976).
If the stay is denied, Mr. Jennings will suffer irreparable harm. The balance of 
equities weighs overwhelmingly in favor of preserving his life until this Court can 
determine whether Florida’s process comports with the Constitution. Florida’s 
interest in finality is outweighed by Mr. Jennings’ continuing interest in life and his 
right to be executed, if at all, under constitutionally valid procedures. See Ohio Adult 
Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 272, 289 (1998) (O’Connor, J., concurring) (“It is 
incorrect . . . to say that a prisoner has been deprived of all interest in his life before 
his execution.”). 
Mr. Jennings’ case raises interrelated constitutional issues of exceptional 
importance. First, Florida’s failure to ensure continuous postconviction counsel 
violates due process and the constitutional guarantee of meaningful access to the 
courts and denies Mr. Jennings of his protected property right in that continuous 
representation. Although state law mandates continuous state postconviction 
representation for all death-sentenced prisoners,1 Mr. Jennings was left with no 
representation in state courts for more than three years. This systemic failure 
transforms Florida’s statutory promise into a right without a remedy and offends the 
basic due process principle that a condemned prisoner must have a fair and 
meaningful opportunity to be heard. See Powell v. Alabama, 287 U.S. 45, 58 (1932). 
The Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments require reliability in capital proceedings, 
1 §§ 27.7001, 27.711(2), Fla. Stat.

4
not perfunctory compliance. Proffitt v. Wainwright, 685 F.2d 1227, 1253 (11th Cir. 
1982). When the State abdicates its statutory responsibility to ensure representation, 
and then imposes impossible deadlines under a death warrant, it deprives the 
condemned of the process and advocacy that are indispensable to constitutional 
reliability.
Second, as detailed in Jennings’ petition for a writ of certiorari, Florida’s 
current capital sentencing scheme violates the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments’ 
demand for fairness, consistency, and evolving standards of decency. Florida now 
stands as an outlier among death penalty jurisdictions. The defects extant in Florida’s 
entire capital sentencing and execution regime, taken together, create a 
constitutionally intolerable risk of arbitrariness, the precise evil condemned in 
Furman v. Georgia, 408 U.S. 238 (1972). Florida’s devolving standards of decency
contravene this Court’s modern Eighth Amendment jurisprudence, which requires 
that the death penalty evolve toward greater fairness. Trop v. Dulles, 356 U.S. 86, 
101 (1958).
Execution is the quintessential form of irreparable harm. Wainwright v. 
Booker, 473 U.S. 935, 937 n.1 (1985) (Powell, J., concurring). Once carried out, the 
constitutional violations identified in this case – Mr. Jennings’ case – will forever 
escape review. The balance of equities and public interest therefore weigh decisively 
in favor of a stay. Florida’s asserted interest in finality is minimal compared to the 
constitutional and moral interest in ensuring that the ultimate punishment is 
imposed only after full and fair process. See Woodard, 523 U.S. at 289. The

5
irreparable harm to Mr. Jennings is clear. Allowing this execution to proceed would 
erode public confidence in the justice system and place Florida further outside the 
bounds of national consensus. 
By broadening death eligibility, lowering procedural thresholds, and bestowing 
more privacy rights to the executive clemency and warrant processes, Florida has 
transformed the death penalty from an exceptional punishment reserved for the most 
aggravated cases into a routine sentencing option, to be carried out perfunctorily, 
expeditiously, and without conscience.
This Court has repeatedly intervened when death sentenced defendants face 
execution under procedures that undermine due process and fundamental fairness. 
See Furman, 408 U.S. at 238; Gregg, 428 U.S. at 153. Mr. Jennings’ case presents 
analogous structural violations, including the denial of counsel, deprivation of 
meaningful access, and regression from established Eighth Amendment protections, 
that strike at the heart of constitutional reliability. There is at least a significant 
possibility that the lower court’s decision will be reversed. See Barefoot, 463 U.S. at 
888.
While the rest of society’s standards of decency are evolving, the Florida courts 
have continued and will continue to foreclose relief in other similar cases and return 
Florida to its outlier status as regards the death penalty. This creates an 
unacceptable risk that other similarly situated individuals will also be denied their 
crucial Sixth, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendment protections.

6
As detailed in Mr. Jennings’ contemporaneous petition for a writ of certiorari, 
this Court’s intervention is urgently needed prevent the imminent execution of Mr. 
Jennings, a man who has been deprived of counsel and meaningful access to the 
courts at a critical stage in his proceedings, but who is nonetheless deserving of the 
protections provided by the Sixth, Eighth, and Fourteenth Amendments of the United 
States Constitution. The Florida Supreme Court refuses to supply these 
constitutional protections; as a result, this Court should grant a stay of execution and 
grant a writ of certiorari.

7
CONCLUSION
“A fundamental requirement of due process is the ‘opportunity to be heard’…at 
a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.’” Armstrong v. Manzo, 380 U.S. 545, 
552 (1965). Mr. Jennings’ meritorious issues cannot possibly be heard in a meaningful 
manner with just days left until his execution. The important constitutional issues 
presented by Mr. Jennings’ case require a full appellate review that is not truncated 
by his imminent execution. 
Because the constitutional questions presented are substantial, the equities 
weigh decisively in favor of relief, and the harm to Mr. Jennings would be irreparable,
Mr. Jennings respectfully requests that this Court grant his application for a stay of 
his execution scheduled for November 13, 2025, to address the compelling 
constitutional questions in his case.
Respectfully submitted,
/s/ Eric C. Pinkard
